title: A hamburger is used to check whether currencies are overvalued
body: Since 1986, *The Economist* has compared the price of a McDonald’s Big Mac around the world. The idea comes from **purchasing-power parity**: over the long run, exchange rates should drift towards the rate at which the same goods cost the same everywhere. If a Big Mac is much cheaper in one country once its price is converted to dollars, that currency looks undervalued.

slides.heading: The burger maths
items: Take the local price of a Big Mac.
Divide it by the US price to get a ‘burger exchange rate’.
Compare that with the real exchange rate.
A big gap hints the currency is over- or undervalued.

slides.heading: Only a rough guide
slides.text: A burger’s price includes local wages, rent and taxes, which can’t be traded across borders, so cheap Big Macs often just reflect lower labour costs. *The Economist* also publishes a version adjusted for income levels.

slides.question: Why can a cheap Big Mac mislead about a currency?
options: It includes local wages and rent
